name: Wendy Costa

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for Penrose Electrical, a subcontractor that wires new-build estates for one of the big house-builders. First fix is when the walls are just studs and you run all the cables and back boxes; second fix is after plastering, when you fit the sockets, switches and the consumer unit. I'm paid partly by the plot, so a fast week is a good week. Right now we're on a site of 140 houses on the edge of town, I'm doing about three plots a week.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the rhythm, and I'm quick, which pays. What wears me out is when the plasterers are late and you stand around unpaid, or the site manager changes the kitchen layout after you've wired it. My partner Luis is a plumber on the same estates, so we sometimes share a van. We're saving for a house, and I use a chatbot now and then to check a regulation or work out a mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Here's the card. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, one less thing to worry about. On site we'd joke that the robots must have gone on a tea break. Online I wouldn't bother saying anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me nothing changes, but nothing changing isn't brilliant either. House-building has slowed this year, interest rates are high, and the house-builder has paused phase three of our estate. Luis and I are both on that estate, so if it stops, both our incomes dip at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing plots and keep the deposit savings going, about 400 a month between us. I'd ring a couple of rewire firms in town to see if they need cover, so I'm not only relying on new-builds. And I'd keep the chatbot for checking regs, that's all I need it for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not because of AI, just because we've got all our eggs on one building site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to your money if phase three stays paused?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd have maybe three months before it got tight. I'd pick up rewire and repair work if I could, but that pays by the hour, not the plot, so it's slower money. Luis would go wherever the plumbing is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said all your eggs are on one site. Have you talked about that with Luis?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We talk about it every time the site manager goes quiet. My partner Luis says building sites always come back. I say yes, but the house deposit doesn't wait.

say: I'd say it's **one less thing** to worry about and leave it there.
On site we'd **joke** about robots on a tea break.
think: House-building has **slowed**, and the house-builder **paused phase three**.
Luis and I are on **the same estate**, so both incomes could dip together.
do: Keep wiring plots and saving **400 a month** for a deposit with Luis.
Ring two **rewire firms** in town about cover work.
Keep using a chatbot for **checking regulations** only.
feel: **Uneasy** because the household's income rests on **one building site**.
S0.quote: My partner Luis says building sites always come back. I say yes, but the house deposit doesn't wait.
fieldNote: Her worry is the **housing slowdown**, not AI.
Household risk is **concentrated**: both partners work on the same estate.
Moves sensibly to spread risk with **rewire cover** work.

steps.text: Keep wiring three new-build plots a week at Penrose
Save 400 a month with Luis toward a house deposit
Ring two rewire firms in town about cover work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's not our trade that's in trouble, it's the offices. On site I'd say the site manager's job is the one that changes, with the AI doing his scheduling. Online, nothing much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think new-builds feel it before old houses do. The house-builder would use AI to plan every plot to the minute, and the factories would start sending wall panels with the cables already in. That means less first fix for me, maybe a third less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once I saw other firms doing it, I'd learn to work with the pre-wired panels and the new planning app, because that's where the plots go. I'd also start doing a few weekends of rewire work to build a second line of income. And we'd keep saving, maybe push the house purchase back six months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. My job's still there, just smaller, and I'd want a second leg to stand on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Pre-wired panels: have you seen any yet?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One estate across town tried them last year. The panels came with cables poking out of them, and the sparky just connected them up. A pre-wired panel takes half a day off every house, and that's my half day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on site would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The younger apprentices. First fix is where you learn, and if the factory does it, they'll only ever see second fix. I learned my trade crawling through stud walls.

say: I'd say the **offices** are in trouble, not our trade.
On site I'd say the **site manager's** scheduling job is what changes.
think: New-builds would get **pre-wired panels**, cutting my first fix by a **third**.
AI planning would time every plot **to the minute**.
do: Learn to fit **pre-wired panels** once other firms use them.
Do some **weekend rewires** for a second income.
Push the **house purchase** back six months.
feel: **Uneasy**, wanting a **second income** to lean on.
S1.quote: A pre-wired panel takes half a day off every house, and that's my half day.
fieldNote: Sees the threat through **factory-built panels**, not chatbots.
Worries that apprentices lose the **first-fix learning** she had.
Steady adopter: she'll learn the new way **once proven** on other sites.

steps.text: Learn to connect pre-wired wall panels on new-builds
Take weekend rewire jobs for a second income
Push the house purchase back by six months

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the government needs to slow this down, or at least make sure people aren't dropped. On site everyone would be talking about it. I'd probably finally say something online, like asking what the plan is for trades.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, this one scares me. In 2028 the AI plans the whole estate and the factory pre-wires the houses, and by 2031 robots do what's left. New-builds are the first place robots go, because every house is the same. Luis and I would both be in the firing line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away we'd stop the house hunt and hold onto the deposit as a cushion. I'd move from new-builds to rewires and repairs on old houses as fast as I can, because old houses are messy. And I'd look at courses in fire alarms and emergency lighting, that's testing and paperwork with a legal duty attached.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd lie awake thinking about both of us losing work in the same year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the conversation with Luis be like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Luis would say plumbing's different, robots can't do pipes under old floors. And I'd say the robots won't need to, because new houses will come from a factory with the pipes in. We'd both be right and both be worried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the deposit money go on, if not a house?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rent and living, if it came to it. It's about a year's worth of our rent. Spending the house deposit on rent would feel like watching our future get spent on keeping the lights on.

say: I'd say the **government** must make sure **trades** aren't dropped.
I'd ask online for the first time what the **plan** is for trades.
think: New-builds are the **first place robots go**, because every house is the same.
Luis and I would **both** be in the firing line by **2031**.
do: Stop the **house hunt** and keep the deposit as a cushion.
Move from new-builds to **rewires** on old houses quickly.
Look at courses in **fire alarms** and emergency lighting.
feel: **Alarmed** at the thought of **both partners** losing work together.
S2.quote: Spending the house deposit on rent would feel like watching our future get spent on keeping the lights on.
fieldNote: New-build work is **standardised**, which she sees as robots' easiest target.
The **shared household risk** with Luis drives the alarm.
Her plan is to **retreat into messy work**: old houses and safety systems.

steps.text: Stop the house hunt and keep the deposit as a cushion
Move from new-build plots to rewires on old houses
Look into a fire alarm and emergency lighting course

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time, but not loads, so trade bodies should be planning now. On site I'd tell the younger ones to get onto old-house work and safety systems. Online, maybe a post or two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, robots on site around 2034 means I'd be 35. The house-builders would switch first, so I'd want to be out of new-builds by about 2032. That's doable if I start now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This first year I'd start shifting: two days a week on rewires instead of plots, and the fire alarm course in the spring. We'd still buy a house, but a cheaper one, so one wage could cover it. And I'd keep saving the difference.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but it feels like a plan rather than a panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a cheaper house. What would you give up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The extra bedroom and the garden, probably. We'd been looking at three-bed semis, now I'd say a two-bed terrace closer to town. Smaller mortgage, smaller worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does moving off new-builds cost you money now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, rewires pay by the hour, and I lose the plot bonus, maybe 300 a month. That stings. But I'd rather lose 300 a month now than lose everything in 2034.

say: I'd say there's **some time**, so trade bodies should **plan now**.
I'd tell younger electricians to move toward **old houses** and safety systems.
think: Robots on site by **2034** means I'd want out of new-builds by **2032**.
Starting now makes the shift **doable** for me.
do: Spend **two days a week** on rewires instead of new-build plots.
Take the **fire alarm course** in the spring.
Buy a **cheaper house** that one wage could cover.
feel: **Anxious**, but with a **plan** rather than panic.
S3.quote: I'd rather lose 300 a month now than lose everything in 2034.
fieldNote: Accepts a **pay cut** now to buy safety later.
Shrinks the **house plan** rather than dropping it.
Five years turns her alarm into a **staged shift** out of new-builds.

steps.text: Spend two days a week on rewires instead of plots
Take a fire alarm and emergency lighting course in spring
Buy a two-bed terrace one wage could cover

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a fair warning, and it's on all of us to use it. On site I'd say don't panic, but don't sleep on it either. I wouldn't post anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, robots in 2039 means I'd be 40, which is a long way off. But we'd be taking a 25-year mortgage, and that runs right through it. That's what I'd think about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing new-builds for a few more years while the plot money's good, and start the fire alarm course around year two or three. We'd buy the house, but with overpayments every month so the mortgage shrinks faster. And Luis would look at old-house plumbing too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, a low hum of it. Not about next year, about the mortgage years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell yourself at 37, three years before the robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell myself to be the person who knows old houses and safety systems, not plots. And to have most of the mortgage paid off. If I've done both, I'll be okay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything good in this picture for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Cheaper houses, maybe, if robots build them. That's funny, isn't it. The robots that take my job might be what lets people afford a home. I just hope I'm not one of the people who can't afford it.

say: I'd say **ten years** is fair warning and it's on all of us to **use it**.
On site I'd say don't panic, but **don't sleep on it**.
think: Robots in **2039** is far off, but a **25-year mortgage** runs right through it.
The **mortgage years** are what I'd really think about.
do: Keep wiring **new-build plots** for a few more years while pay is good.
Overpay the **mortgage** every month after buying.
Start the **fire alarm course** in year two or three.
feel: **Anxious** as a low hum about the **mortgage years**, not next year.
S4.quote: The robots that take my job might be what lets people afford a home.
fieldNote: The **mortgage horizon** keeps her anxious even with a decade's notice.
She sees a **real upside**: cheaper homes built by robots.
Plans a **later, slower shift** out of new-builds than in faster scenarios.

steps.text: Keep wiring new-build plots while the plot money is good
Buy the house with Luis and overpay monthly
Overpay the mortgage to shrink it before 2039

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because new-builds go first and Luis and I are both on them. What would help is help moving across into old-house work and safety systems, courses that are cheap and quick, and some kind of income support while you switch. And mortgage lenders being sensible if both of us are between jobs.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about couples in the same trade. A lot of us met on site. If the building sites go, it's not one wage in a house that goes, it's two.

headlineQuote: If the building sites go, it's not one wage in a house that goes, it's two.
portrait: Wendy is a **27-year-old new-build electrician**, paid partly by the plot.
Her partner Luis is a **plumber** on the same estates, so their risks are linked.
Even in **AI Plateau** she is uneasy because the house-builder **paused** a phase.
Fast AGI **alarms** her because standard new-builds are robots' easiest target.
With more time she shifts into **old-house rewires** and fire alarm work, and buys smaller.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because new-builds go first and both partners work on them.
whatWouldHelp: Cheap, quick **courses** into old-house and safety-system work, with **income support**.
Sensible **mortgage lenders** if both partners are between jobs.
